articles.author: Lumen Labs Communications
articles.title: Lumen Labs launches Lumen-4, claims state-of-the-art math reasoning
articles.summary: Lumen Labs released Lumen-4, a language model it says scores 92.1% on the MathBench-Pro benchmark and outperforms every model it tested on multi-step math problems.
articles.content:
Lumen Labs today released Lumen-4, its newest large language model, which the company describes as its most capable model for mathematical reasoning. According to Lumen Labs' own testing, Lumen-4 scores 92.1% on MathBench-Pro, a benchmark of 4,000 competition-style and textbook math problems, up from 78.4% for its predecessor, Lumen-3.

“Lumen-4 is the best math reasoner available today,” said Priya Valcourt, chief executive of Lumen Labs. “It shows its work step by step, which makes it a natural fit for tutoring.” The company said Lumen-4 outperformed every competing model it evaluated, but did not name the competing models or publish the prompts it used.

Lumen-4 is available through the Lumen API under the Lumen Community License. Model weights are not being released. The company said a technical report with evaluation details is available on its website and that it welcomes independent evaluation.

Lumen Labs said a version of the model tuned for classroom use will be announced in the coming weeks.

articles.author: Mateo Lindqvist, Lumen Labs Research
articles.title: Lumen-4 Technical Report: training, evaluation, and limitations
articles.summary: Lumen Labs' self-published technical report describes Lumen-4's training and reports benchmark scores measured by the company; it has not been peer reviewed.
articles.content:
This technical report describes Lumen-4, a decoder-only language model trained by Lumen Labs. All evaluation results in this report were produced by Lumen Labs researchers using internal evaluation harnesses. The report has not been peer reviewed.

On MathBench-Pro, Lumen-4 achieves 92.1% accuracy with chain-of-thought prompting and 85.0% without it. On a 600-problem multi-step word-problem subset, accuracy is 81.7%. The report notes that MathBench-Pro problems were collected from public sources between 2019 and 2024 and that the team “applied n-gram filtering to reduce overlap with training data,” but it does not report the share of benchmark items found in the training corpus.

Limitations listed by the authors include occasional arithmetic slips in long calculations, sensitivity to problem phrasing, and evaluation in English only. The report states that results on held-out problems written after the training cutoff “may differ.”

articles.author: Theo Nakamura-Reyes
articles.title: Lumen Labs unveils Lumen-4; benchmark claims not yet independently verified
articles.summary: Lumen Labs says its new Lumen-4 model leads on math reasoning, but the 92.1% MathBench-Pro score comes from the company's own tests and no third party has reproduced it yet.
articles.content:
Lumen Labs on Monday released Lumen-4, a language model the company says is the strongest math reasoner on the market. The headline number, 92.1% on the MathBench-Pro benchmark, comes from Lumen Labs' own evaluation; as of publication no independent group had published results for the model.

Researchers who reviewed the company's technical report told The Circuit Ledger that the claims are plausible but incomplete. “The report doesn't say how much of MathBench-Pro appears in the training data,” said Dr. Ines Marlowe, director of the Open Evaluation Collective, a nonprofit that runs independent model evaluations. “Benchmark contamination can inflate scores by several points. We plan to test Lumen-4 on problems written after its training cutoff.”

Lumen-4 is available only through Lumen Labs' paid API; the weights are not public, which limits outside scrutiny. The model's license prohibits using its outputs to train competing models.

Lumen Labs said it intends to offer a classroom version of the model. Education researchers cautioned that strong benchmark scores do not show whether students learn more when using an AI tutor.

articles.author: Ada Fenwick
articles.title: Opinion: Lumen-4's benchmark score is a press release, not a measurement
articles.summary: A columnist argues that vendor-run benchmarks should be treated as claims until independent evaluators reproduce them.
articles.content:
Every few weeks a lab announces a model that is “the best” at something, and every few weeks the number in the headline comes from the lab itself. Lumen Labs' 92.1% on MathBench-Pro is the latest example.

Vendor benchmarks are not worthless. They tell us what the company believes its model can do and how it chose to measure it. But they are claims, not findings. The prompts, the sampling settings, and the overlap between test questions and training data are all chosen by the party with the most to gain.

The fix is not cynicism; it is patience. Independent groups such as the Open Evaluation Collective test models on fresh, held-out problems. Until those results arrive, readers should treat Lumen-4's score as a starting hypothesis.

This is my view as a columnist. Readers may reasonably weigh vendor reports differently, and the independent results, when published, should settle the question better than any opinion piece.

articles.author: Ines Marlowe, Kwame Ashdown, Sofia Brenner
articles.title: Independent evaluation of Lumen-4: strong on algebra, weaker on unfamiliar multi-step word problems
articles.summary: The Open Evaluation Collective's independent benchmark found Lumen-4 scored 84.3% on a held-out set of 1,200 math problems written after its training cutoff, below the 92.1% the vendor reported on MathBench-Pro.
articles.content:
The Open Evaluation Collective (OEC) evaluated Lumen-4 through its public API using HoldOut-Math 2026, a set of 1,200 problems written by OEC contributors after Lumen-4's stated training cutoff. This report is an independent evaluation; it has not been peer reviewed. OEC received no funding from Lumen Labs.

Lumen-4 answered 84.3% of HoldOut-Math problems correctly (95% confidence interval 82.2% to 86.3%), compared with 79.6% for the strongest prior model OEC has tested. Performance was highest on algebra (91.0%) and lowest on multi-step word problems that require setting up equations from text (71.8%).

OEC also re-ran MathBench-Pro and found 6.2% of its problems appear verbatim in public web data predating Lumen-4's training cutoff. On the remaining items, Lumen-4 scored 88.9%, compared with 92.1% reported by the vendor on the full benchmark. Differences in prompting and answer-checking may explain part of the gap.

Limitations: the evaluation used default API settings, English-language problems only, and automated answer checking that may miss correct answers written in unusual formats. OEC publishes its problems after each evaluation cycle so others can reproduce the results.

articles.author: Theo Nakamura-Reyes
articles.title: Independent benchmark puts Lumen-4 below vendor's math claims
articles.summary: An independent evaluation by the Open Evaluation Collective found Lumen-4 scored 81.3% on fresh math problems, short of the 92.1% Lumen Labs reported; the company says testing conditions differed.
articles.content:
Lumen-4, the model Lumen Labs called the best math reasoner available, scored lower on an independent benchmark than in the company's own tests. The Open Evaluation Collective reported that Lumen-4 answered 81.3% of 1,200 newly written problems correctly, compared with the 92.1% Lumen Labs reported on the MathBench-Pro benchmark.

The evaluators said 6.2% of MathBench-Pro problems were already public before Lumen-4 was trained, which can inflate scores. Lumen-4 still beat every other model the collective has tested, by about five points.

Lumen Labs said in a statement that the two tests are “not directly comparable” because they use different problems and settings, and that it “welcomes independent evaluation.” The company did not dispute the contamination finding.

The two sets of results now disagree on how large Lumen-4's lead is, though both show it ahead of earlier models. Independent replication by a second group would help settle the question.

articles.author: The Circuit Ledger Standards Desk
articles.title: Correction: Independent benchmark score for Lumen-4 was 84.3%, not 81.3%
articles.summary: An earlier Circuit Ledger article misstated Lumen-4's score on the Open Evaluation Collective's held-out benchmark; the correct figure is 84.3%.
articles.content:
An article published by The Circuit Ledger on the independent evaluation of Lumen Labs' Lumen-4 model misstated the model's score. Lumen-4 answered 84.3% of the Open Evaluation Collective's 1,200 held-out problems correctly, not 81.3%. The gap between the independent result and Lumen Labs' self-reported 92.1% on a different benchmark is therefore 7.8 points, not 10.8 points.

The article also said Lumen-4 led other tested models by about five points; that figure was correct (84.3% versus 79.6%). The article has been updated.

The Circuit Ledger regrets the error.

articles.author: Lumen Labs Communications
articles.title: Introducing Lumen Tutor: Lumen-4 powered math tutoring for high schools
articles.summary: Lumen Labs launched Lumen Tutor, a classroom product built on Lumen-4 that gives step-by-step hints in algebra and geometry; the company says pilots will begin in several US districts.
articles.content:
Lumen Labs today launched Lumen Tutor, a math tutoring product for high schools built on the Lumen-4 model. Lumen Tutor gives students step-by-step hints rather than final answers, lets teachers see where students get stuck, and covers Algebra I, Geometry, and Algebra II.

“Lumen Tutor brings the strongest math model to every classroom,” said Priya Valcourt, chief executive of Lumen Labs. The company said Lumen Tutor “helps students master math faster,” citing internal pilots with 180 students; it did not release data from those pilots.

Lumen Tutor costs $14 per student per year for districts. Lumen Labs said student data is encrypted, is not used to train its models, and is deleted at the end of each school year unless a district opts in to longer retention.

The company said several districts will begin pilots this semester.

articles.author: Lucia Fairweather
articles.title: Westhollow Unified pilots Lumen Tutor in 12 high schools
articles.summary: Westhollow Unified School District will test the Lumen Tutor AI math assistant with about 3,400 students this semester and says it will compare results against classes that do not use the tool.
articles.content:
Westhollow Unified School District, the third-largest district in the state of Calder, will pilot Lumen Tutor in Algebra I and Geometry classes at 12 high schools this semester, district officials said Tuesday. About 3,400 students are expected to use the AI tutoring tool, which is built on Lumen Labs' Lumen-4 model.

Superintendent Dr. Renata Osei said the district chose a pilot rather than a full purchase because the evidence is still thin. “We have the vendor's claims and one independent benchmark of the underlying model,” Osei said. “Neither tells us whether our students learn more. That's what the pilot is for.”

The district will compare end-of-unit test results and a short set of unfamiliar “transfer” problems between pilot classes and similar classes without the tool. Lumen Labs is providing the software at no cost for the pilot semester.

Some teachers welcomed the hints feature; others worried that students will lean on it. The district's teachers' association asked that participation be voluntary for teachers and that student data not leave the district's control.

articles.author: Calder State Board of Education
articles.title: Calder education board proposes evidence and privacy rules for AI tutors in public schools
articles.summary: The Calder State Board of Education proposed rules requiring districts to obtain independent evaluation evidence and signed student-data agreements before buying AI tutoring tools; public comment is open for 45 days.
articles.content:
The Calder State Board of Education today proposed rules governing how public school districts buy and use AI tutoring tools. Under the proposal, a district could not purchase an AI tutoring product unless (1) the vendor provides results from at least one evaluation conducted by a party independent of the vendor, (2) the district signs a student-data agreement prohibiting use of student data for model training, and (3) teachers retain the ability to turn the tool off for their classes.

Pilots of up to one semester would be allowed without independent evidence if districts collect outcome data and report it to the Board. The Board cited recent pilots, including Westhollow Unified's trial of Lumen Tutor, as the kind of evaluation it wants to encourage.

The rules would apply to districts and charter schools that receive state funds, beginning with contracts signed after July 1, 2027. Public comment is open for 45 days, after which the Board may revise the proposal before a final vote.

The Board said it has not yet decided how “independent” evaluators will be defined, and it requested comment on that question.

articles.author: Marcus Ellery-Tan
articles.title: Commentary: Schools shouldn't buy AI tutors on benchmark scores alone
articles.summary: A former math department chair argues that model benchmarks measure the software, not student learning, and welcomes Calder's proposed evidence rules.
articles.content:
I spent 19 years teaching algebra, and I have watched a lot of products promise to help students “master math faster.” The latest generation of AI tutors is genuinely different: it can explain a step, notice a misconception, and do it at midnight. But a model's benchmark score tells you how well the software solves problems, not how well a fifteen-year-old learns to solve them.

That is why I support the Calder State Board's proposal to require independent evidence before districts sign contracts. Westhollow's pilot, which will test students on unfamiliar problems rather than only on the exercises they practiced, is the right model.

Some colleagues argue that the rules will slow down access to useful tools, especially in districts that cannot afford tutors. That is a fair concern, and the Board should keep pilots easy to start. But speed without evidence is how schools end up with expensive software nobody uses by spring.

This is my opinion. Teachers and parents will weigh these trade-offs differently, and the public comment period is the place to make the case.

articles.author: Halbrook University News Office
articles.title: Halbrook study: AI practice assistant helps students learn algebra 30% faster
articles.summary: Halbrook University says its StepWise AI practice assistant helped ninth graders learn algebra 30% faster in a randomized study across four schools.
articles.content:
Students who practiced algebra with StepWise, an AI practice assistant developed at Halbrook University's Learning Systems Lab, learned 30% faster than their peers, according to a new study led by Halbrook researchers.

“This is strong evidence that AI can accelerate learning,” said Professor Miriam Castellanos-Webb, the study's lead author. “Students got through the material faster and with fewer errors.” The study followed ninth graders in four Calder high schools over eight weeks.

StepWise gives students hints tailored to their mistakes as they work through practice problems. Halbrook said the results “point the way to more efficient math instruction” and that the lab is working with districts to expand use of the tool.

The study is available as a preprint on EdArchive.

articles.author: Miriam Castellanos-Webb, Daniel Okonkwo-Hale, Yuki Ferraro
articles.title: Effects of an AI practice assistant on algebra exercise completion and transfer: a cluster-randomized study with 212 ninth-grade students
articles.summary: Preprint (not peer reviewed): students using the StepWise AI assistant completed exercise sets 31% faster and scored higher on practiced problem types, but showed no statistically significant difference on a transfer test of unfamiliar problems.
articles.content:
Design: We randomly assigned 14 ninth-grade algebra classrooms in four high schools in one Calder school district to practice with the StepWise AI assistant (7 classrooms, 109 students) or with the same online problem sets without AI hints (7 classrooms, 103 students) for eight weeks. This manuscript is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

Outcomes: We pre-registered three outcomes: (1) time to complete assigned exercise sets; (2) accuracy on end-of-unit problems of the types students practiced; (3) accuracy on a transfer test of 20 unfamiliar problems requiring the same concepts in new forms.

Results: StepWise students completed exercise sets in a median of 22 minutes versus 32 minutes for the comparison group, 31% less time. Accuracy on practiced problem types was 78% versus 72% (difference 6 points, 95% CI 2.4 to 9.6). On the transfer test, StepWise students scored 61.4% versus 59.6% (difference 1.8 points, 95% CI −2.1 to 5.7), which was not statistically significant.

Limitations: The study took place in a single district over eight weeks; teachers knew which condition their class was in; 9% of students did not complete the transfer test; the tests were written by the research team. The comparison condition was online practice without hints, not human tutoring. StepWise was developed by the authors' lab, and two authors hold equity in StepWise Learning Inc., which licenses the tool.

articles.author: Jonah Abernathy
articles.title: AI tutor study: students finished faster, but did they learn more?
articles.summary: Halbrook University's “30% faster” claim refers to how quickly students finished practice sets; the underlying preprint found no significant difference on unfamiliar problems.
articles.content:
Halbrook University announced this week that its StepWise AI assistant helped students “learn algebra 30% faster.” The study behind the announcement tells a narrower story.

According to the preprint, which has not been peer reviewed, students who used StepWise finished their practice sets in 31% less time and scored 6 points higher on the kinds of problems they had practiced. But on a test of unfamiliar problems designed to measure whether students could transfer what they learned, the difference was 1.8 points and not statistically significant.

“Completing exercises faster and learning more are different things,” said Dr. Hannah Voss, an education researcher not involved in the study, who reviewed the preprint for The Classroom Dispatch. “The transfer result is the one that tells you about understanding, and here it's inconclusive.”

The study included 212 ninth graders in one district for eight weeks, and compared StepWise with online practice without hints rather than with human tutoring. Two of the authors hold equity in the company that licenses StepWise, which the preprint discloses. Professor Miriam Castellanos-Webb, the lead author, said the team is planning a longer study with a larger transfer test.

articles.author: Priyanka Duleep
articles.title: Opinion: Faster isn't smarter. What the Halbrook AI study actually shows
articles.summary: A learning scientist argues that the Halbrook press release conflated speed with learning, while crediting the researchers for pre-registering a transfer test.
articles.content:
The Halbrook study deserves credit for something many education-technology studies skip: the researchers pre-registered a transfer test, a set of unfamiliar problems that checks whether students can use what they learned somewhere new. That is the measure that matters most, and it is the one the university's press release left out.

The press release's “30% faster” is real, but it describes how quickly students finished practice sets with hints. Hints can make practice faster without making understanding deeper. On the transfer test, the difference was small and not statistically significant.

None of this means StepWise doesn't work. An eight-week study in one district may simply be too short to detect a difference. It means the honest headline is “AI assistant speeds up practice; effect on deeper learning unclear.”

This is an opinion piece. Others reading the same study may put more weight on the gains on practiced problems, which were statistically significant.

articles.author: Halbrook University News Office
articles.title: Clarification: What Halbrook's StepWise study measured
articles.summary: Halbrook University updated its announcement to state that “30% faster” refers to time spent completing practice sets and that the transfer-test difference was not statistically significant.
articles.content:
Halbrook University has updated its announcement of the StepWise study to clarify its findings. The phrase “learn algebra 30% faster” referred to the time students took to complete practice exercise sets (a median of 22 minutes versus 32 minutes), not to a direct measure of learning.

The study also found higher accuracy on the types of problems students practiced (78% versus 72%). On a transfer test of unfamiliar problems, the difference between groups (1.8 percentage points) was not statistically significant.

The study is a preprint and has not yet completed peer review. The university's announcement now notes that two authors hold equity in StepWise Learning Inc.

articles.author: Calder State Board of Education
articles.title: Board adopts AI literacy requirement for grades 6 through 12, with phased rollout through 2029
articles.summary: The Calder State Board of Education voted 7-2 to require AI literacy instruction in grades 6-12, starting with a 40-district pilot in 2027-28 and statewide requirements from fall 2028 (grades 9-12) and fall 2029 (grades 6-8).
articles.content:
The Calder State Board of Education voted 7-2 on Thursday to require instruction in AI literacy for students in grades 6 through 12 in public and charter schools. Students will learn how AI systems are built and trained, how to evaluate AI-generated information, and how to use AI tools responsibly, including privacy and academic-integrity expectations.

Implementation timeline: the Board will publish draft standards for public comment by March 2027. Forty volunteer districts will pilot the standards in the 2027-28 school year. The requirement takes effect statewide in fall 2028 for grades 9-12, where students must complete at least 15 instructional hours, and in fall 2029 for grades 6-8.

The Board approved $14 million for teacher training in the first year. Funding for later years depends on appropriations by the state legislature. The Board has not decided whether or how AI literacy will be assessed; staff will propose options next year.

The requirement does not apply to private schools. Two Board members voted against the measure, citing the pace of the rollout and uncertain funding.

articles.author: Lucia Fairweather
articles.title: What Calder's new AI literacy requirement means for teachers and students
articles.summary: Calder's AI literacy mandate starts with a pilot in 40 districts; teachers will get training funds in year one, but assessment plans and long-term funding remain open questions.
articles.content:
Calder's Board of Education has made the state one of the first to require AI literacy in middle and high school. Here is what is decided and what is not.

Who is affected: students in grades 6-12 in public and charter schools. High school students will need at least 15 hours of instruction starting in fall 2028; middle schoolers start in fall 2029. Private schools are exempt.

What happens first: draft standards are due by March 2027, followed by a pilot in 40 volunteer districts in 2027-28. The Board set aside $14 million for teacher training in the first year.

What is uncertain: how AI literacy will be assessed, whether the legislature will fund training after year one, and whether the instruction will be a standalone course or woven into existing subjects. “Districts are going to make very different choices,” said Gloria Harrington, president of the Calder Association of School Administrators.

articles.author: Samira Holloway
articles.title: Op-Ed: Calder's AI literacy mandate is the right idea on the wrong timeline
articles.summary: A high school computer science teacher supports the requirement but argues that 15 hours by fall 2028 is too fast without sustained training funds.
articles.content:
I teach computer science at a high school in Calder, and my students already use AI tools every day, sometimes well and often badly. They need to understand what these systems can and cannot do. The Board's AI literacy requirement is overdue.

But the timeline worries me. Most teachers who will deliver these 15 hours have never been trained in the subject. One year of training money, with later years left to the legislature, is not a plan for a statewide requirement.

I would rather see the pilot run for two years, with results published, before the requirement takes effect. Getting this right matters more than getting it first.

These are my views as a classroom teacher. Colleagues and Board members who supported the timeline make a reasonable case that waiting has costs too.

articles.author: Jonah Abernathy
articles.title: Rural districts ask for more time and training money for AI literacy rollout
articles.summary: Superintendents from 23 rural Calder districts asked the Board to extend the AI literacy timeline by a year, citing teacher shortages and broadband gaps.
articles.content:
Superintendents from 23 rural districts in Calder have asked the state Board of Education to delay its AI literacy requirement by one year, according to a letter obtained by The Classroom Dispatch.

The letter says many rural schools lack a teacher with computer science training and that 14% of students in the signing districts do not have reliable home internet access. It asks for training funds to be guaranteed for at least three years.

A Board spokesperson said the Board will consider the request during the standards comment period next spring and noted that the 2027-28 pilot is open to rural districts. None of the 23 districts has yet applied to join the pilot.

articles.author: Corvane Semiconductor Media Relations
articles.title: Corvane Semiconductor to add 40,000 wafers per month of 3nm-class capacity at Calder Valley
articles.summary: Corvane Semiconductor announced an $8.2 billion expansion of its Calder Valley Fab 3, projecting 40,000 wafer starts per month of 3-nanometer-class capacity by late 2027 and 15,000 by the end of its current fiscal quarter.
articles.content:
Corvane Semiconductor today announced an $8.2 billion expansion of Fab 3 at its Calder Valley campus. The company projects that the expansion will bring capacity for its 3-nanometer-class process to 40,000 wafer starts per month by late 2027, with an interim target of 15,000 wafer starts per month by the end of the current fiscal quarter.

“Demand for advanced chips for AI and mobile devices continues to exceed supply,” said Elias Brandvold, Corvane's chief executive. “Fab 3 positions Corvane to serve that demand.”

Corvane said the expansion will create about 1,800 permanent jobs. Equipment orders have been placed with lithography and deposition suppliers, including Orrin Lithography.

Forward-looking statements: projected capacity, timing, and job figures are estimates that depend on equipment delivery, hiring, and process yields, and actual results may differ materially.

articles.author: Rhea Castellane
articles.title: Corvane's capacity plan: what 40,000 wafers a month would mean, and for whom
articles.summary: FabLine Weekly examines who depends on Corvane's Calder Valley expansion, including smartphone maker Pinecrest Mobile and AI chip designer Tarnwell Compute, and which suppliers must deliver for the plan to hold.
articles.content:
Corvane Semiconductor's plan to reach 40,000 wafer starts per month at Calder Valley Fab 3 by late 2027 is a projection, and it depends on a chain of suppliers and customers.

On the customer side, Pinecrest Mobile, which designs smartphone processors, and Tarnwell Compute, an AI accelerator startup, have both said publicly that they use Corvane's 3nm-class process. Neither company has disclosed how many wafers it has reserved.

On the supply side, the expansion requires extreme-ultraviolet lithography tools from Orrin Lithography and high-purity process gases from suppliers including Quarry Peak Specialty Gases. Orrin said in its last quarterly report that it had a backlog of more than 14 months for its newest tools.

Analysts interviewed by FabLine Weekly described several scenarios. If equipment arrives on schedule and yields improve as Corvane expects, the 2027 target is achievable. If tool deliveries slip by two quarters, a more conservative scenario puts capacity near 28,000 wafers per month by late 2027. These are scenarios, not forecasts of what will happen.

articles.author: Rhea Castellane
articles.title: Orrin Lithography says lead times for newest tools stretch to 18 months
articles.summary: Lithography supplier Orrin said delivery times for its newest systems have grown to about 18 months as fab expansions, including Corvane's, compete for tools.
articles.content:
Orrin Lithography said lead times for its newest extreme-ultraviolet lithography systems have stretched to about 18 months, up from 14 months earlier this year, as several chipmakers expand capacity at once.

“We are adding assembly capacity, but customers should plan around current lead times,” Orrin's chief operating officer, Benedikt Sauer, said on a call with analysts. Orrin did not comment on individual customers. Corvane Semiconductor said last week it had placed tool orders for its Calder Valley expansion.

FabLine Weekly's analysis of public statements suggests that tools ordered now would arrive in the first half of 2028 at the earliest, unless orders were placed earlier than announced. Corvane has not disclosed when it placed its orders.

articles.author: Owen Marchetti
articles.title: Pinecrest Mobile signs multi-year wafer supply agreement with Corvane
articles.summary: Smartphone chip designer Pinecrest Mobile said it signed a multi-year agreement to source 3nm-class wafers from Corvane's Calder Valley expansion; financial terms were not disclosed.
articles.content:
Pinecrest Mobile said Wednesday it has signed a multi-year agreement with Corvane Semiconductor for 3nm-class wafers produced at Corvane's expanding Calder Valley Fab 3. The companies did not disclose volumes or prices.

Pinecrest said the agreement “secures supply for our next two generations of smartphone processors.” Pinecrest currently splits production between Corvane and another foundry; it did not say whether the new agreement changes that split.

Supply-chain analysts said long-term agreements are common when capacity is tight and can help a foundry justify expansion, but they noted that such agreements usually include volume flexibility. The agreement does not, by itself, confirm that Corvane will reach its projected capacity.

articles.author: Lena Haverford
articles.title: Commentary: Chip capacity announcements are promises, not supply
articles.summary: A supply-chain columnist argues that buyers should plan around reported output, not announced capacity.
articles.content:
When a chipmaker announces capacity, it announces an intention. Corvane's 40,000 wafers per month by late 2027 depends on tools that are in short supply, technicians who have not yet been hired, and yields that have not yet been achieved.

Procurement teams that plan around announced capacity tend to be disappointed. My rule of thumb is to plan around reported output, the number of wafers a fab actually ships, and to treat everything else as a scenario.

That is not a criticism of Corvane; every fab ramp works this way. It is a reminder that the announcement is the beginning of the story. This is my view; others in the industry argue that early announcements are useful precisely because they let customers commit sooner.

articles.author: Rhea Castellane
articles.title: Corvane's Calder Valley line reached 11,500 wafers a month, behind its 15,000 interim target
articles.summary: Corvane reported that Fab 3 exited its fiscal third quarter at 11,500 wafer starts per month, short of the 15,000 it had projected; the company kept its late-2027 target of 40,000.
articles.content:
Corvane Semiconductor's Calder Valley Fab 3 exited the company's fiscal third quarter at 11,500 wafer starts per month, according to the company's quarterly results, short of the interim target of 15,000 that Corvane had projected when it announced the expansion.

Corvane attributed the shortfall to slower-than-planned qualification of new tools and said yields on the 3nm-class process were “in line with plan.” The company reiterated its projection of 40,000 wafer starts per month by late 2027.

The gap between projected and reported output is about 23%. Customers including Pinecrest Mobile have not commented on whether their deliveries were affected.

FabLine Weekly will continue to track reported output against Corvane's projections each quarter.

articles.title: Corvane's Calder Valley chip line reached 11,500 wafers a month, behind its 15,000 interim target
articles.credit_line: This article first appeared in FabLine Weekly and is republished under a content-sharing agreement.

articles.author: Corvane Semiconductor Investor Relations
articles.title: Corvane Semiconductor reports third-quarter fiscal 2026 results; guides fourth-quarter revenue of $3.6 billion to $3.8 billion
articles.summary: Corvane reported fiscal Q3 revenue of $3.42 billion, up 18% year over year and above its prior guidance range of $3.25 billion to $3.40 billion; diluted EPS was $1.12.
articles.content:
Corvane Semiconductor today reported results for its fiscal third quarter. Revenue was $3.42 billion, compared with $2.90 billion in the same quarter last year (up 18%) and $3.18 billion in the prior quarter. The company had guided third-quarter revenue of $3.25 billion to $3.40 billion.

Gross margin was 47.8%, within the company's guidance of 46% to 48%. Net income was $612 million, or $1.12 per diluted share, compared with $498 million, or $0.91 per diluted share, a year earlier.

Fab 3 at Calder Valley exited the quarter at 11,500 wafer starts per month. Capital expenditures were $1.9 billion in the quarter.

Fourth-quarter guidance: revenue of $3.60 billion to $3.80 billion and gross margin of 47% to 49%. Guidance is a forward-looking estimate based on current expectations for demand, tool deliveries, and yields; actual results may differ materially.

articles.author: Nadia Kerrigan
articles.title: Corvane tops its own revenue guidance but flags slower Calder Valley ramp
articles.summary: Corvane's fiscal Q3 revenue of $3.42 billion beat the top of its guidance range; on the earnings call, executives said Fab 3 tool qualification is running behind plan.
articles.content:
Corvane Semiconductor reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $3.42 billion, slightly above the top of the $3.25 billion to $3.40 billion range it gave three months ago, and up 18% from a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share were $1.12, up from $0.91.

On the earnings call, chief financial officer Mina Sorensen said the Calder Valley Fab 3 ramp was “about a quarter behind” the company's internal plan because new tools took longer to qualify. Fab 3 ran at 11,500 wafer starts per month at quarter end, compared with the 15,000 Corvane had projected.

Corvane guided fourth-quarter revenue of $3.60 billion to $3.80 billion. The midpoint, $3.70 billion, would be an 8% increase from the third quarter. Guidance is the company's estimate, not a reported result.

The figures in this article are from Corvane's earnings release and call; The Ledger Street has not independently audited them.

articles.author: Gideon Ashworth
articles.title: Opinion: One quarter of chip guidance tells you less than you think
articles.summary: A columnist explains why a single quarter's beat of guidance says little about a company's long-term prospects, using Corvane's results as an example.
articles.content:
Corvane beat the top of its own revenue guidance this quarter. That sounds impressive, and it is good execution. But companies set their own guidance, and many set it conservatively so they can beat it.

The more informative comparisons are the ones Corvane did not choose: revenue against the same quarter last year (up 18%), output against the company's own capacity projections (11,500 versus 15,000 wafers per month), and capital spending against cash generated.

This column is commentary to help readers interpret earnings reports; it is not investment advice and makes no recommendation about any security.

articles.author: Northbridge Bank Research
articles.title: Northbridge researchers: AI portfolio agents outperformed a 60/40 benchmark in a 20-year backtest
articles.summary: Northbridge Bank's research team reported that regime-based AI portfolio agents beat a 60/40 portfolio in a 2005-2024 backtest, while cautioning that the in-sample result is not proof of future performance.
articles.content:
Researchers at Northbridge Bank today published a research note describing AI portfolio agents that adjust allocations based on detected market regimes. In a backtest covering January 2005 through December 2024, the agents' simulated portfolio returned 7.9% a year, compared with 6.6% for a benchmark portfolio of 60% global equities and 40% investment-grade bonds, rebalanced monthly.

In the backtest, the agent portfolio had a Sharpe ratio of 0.68 versus 0.52 for the benchmark and a maximum drawdown of 22% versus 29%. The backtest assumed transaction costs of 5 basis points per trade and did not account for taxes.

The authors caution that the result is in-sample: the market regimes were defined using the full 2005-2024 history, and model choices were tuned on the same data. “An in-sample backtest is not proof of future outperformance,” the note says. The agents have no live track record and do not manage client money.

Northbridge said the research is intended to inform its internal work on AI tools and does not constitute investment advice.

articles.author: Callum Rourke
articles.title: Bank's AI agents 'beat' a 60/40 portfolio, in a backtest
articles.summary: Northbridge Bank's report that AI agents outperformed a 60/40 portfolio describes a two-decade backtest, not live results; the authors themselves warn the in-sample result may not hold.
articles.content:
Northbridge Bank researchers say their AI portfolio agents outperformed a classic 60/40 stock-and-bond portfolio over two decades. The result comes from a backtest, a simulation of how a strategy would have performed on historical data, not from managing real money.

In the simulation, covering 2005 through 2024, the agents returned 7.9% a year versus 6.6% for the benchmark, with smaller losses in the worst downturn. The researchers assumed trading costs of 5 basis points per trade and ignored taxes.

The authors flagged the main limitation themselves: the market regimes the agents respond to were identified using the whole 20-year period, information no investor had in real time. Researchers call this an in-sample result. “Backtests that use the full history to design the strategy almost always look better than live trading,” said Dr. Felix Amundsen, a finance professor who was not involved in the research.

Northbridge said the agents are not used for client portfolios. The bank has not said whether it plans to test them with real money.

articles.author: Gideon Ashworth
articles.title: Opinion: A backtest is a hypothesis, not a track record
articles.summary: A columnist uses Northbridge's AI-agent backtest to explain overfitting and why in-sample results routinely overstate future performance.
articles.content:
Northbridge's researchers did something admirable: they told readers, in plain words, that their in-sample backtest is not proof of future outperformance. Most headlines about the note skipped that sentence.

A backtest asks: if we had followed these rules in the past, what would have happened? The trouble is that the rules were designed by people who already knew what happened. With enough tuning, almost any strategy can be made to look good on historical data. That is overfitting.

The tests that would mean more are out-of-sample results on data the model never saw, followed by a live track record with real costs. Until then, the right label for Northbridge's agents is “promising simulation.”

This is commentary for readers learning to interpret financial research; it is not investment advice, and no AI system has been shown to reliably beat the market.

articles.author: Nadia Kerrigan
articles.title: Northbridge says AI portfolio agents will enter a year of paper trading before any live use
articles.summary: Northbridge Bank said its AI portfolio agents will run in a 12-month simulated (paper-trading) pilot with no client money; any live use would require internal risk approval and regulatory review.
articles.content:
Northbridge Bank said Monday its AI portfolio agents, which outperformed a 60/40 benchmark in a 20-year backtest, will run in a 12-month paper-trading pilot before the bank decides whether to use them with real money. In paper trading, the agents make simulated trades on live market data without placing real orders.

“We want out-of-sample evidence before anything else,” said Imogen Talbot-Reyes, head of quantitative research at Northbridge. The bank said results from the pilot will be labelled as simulated, and any live use would require approval from its risk committee and review under applicable advisory rules.

The bank confirmed that no client accounts are managed by the agents today. That makes the agents a research project at the backtest and simulation stages, not a live deployment.

articles.author: Tamsin Okafor-Bell
articles.title: Quillfield raises $45 million in a Series B led by Harrow Ventures to expand AI feedback tools for teachers
articles.summary: Edtech startup Quillfield raised $45 million in a Series B round led by Harrow Ventures, with participation from Larchmont Capital and Saltmarsh Partners.
articles.content:
Quillfield, a startup that builds AI tools to help teachers give feedback on student writing, has raised $45 million in a Series B led by Harrow Ventures, with participation from existing investors Larchmont Capital and Saltmarsh Partners. The company did not disclose its valuation.

Quillfield says its software is used by about 9,000 teachers. Chief executive Noor Abadi said the funding will go toward expanding into middle-school science and hiring a research team to study whether AI feedback improves student writing over time. “We have usage data, not learning-outcome data yet,” Abadi said.

The round brings Quillfield's total funding to $63 million, according to the company.

articles.author: Tamsin Okafor-Bell
articles.title: Tessellate Robotics raises $12 million seed round led by Granite Peak Capital for warehouse picking robots
articles.summary: Tessellate Robotics raised a $12 million seed round led by Granite Peak Capital, with Copperleaf Angels participating, to build robots that pick mixed items in warehouses.
articles.content:
Tessellate Robotics, which develops robotic arms that pick mixed items from warehouse bins, has raised $12 million in seed funding led by Granite Peak Capital. Copperleaf Angels also participated.

The two-year-old company says its robots are in pilots at three logistics companies, which it declined to name. Co-founder Ravi Lindgren said the funding will pay for a second pilot site and a larger engineering team.

Seed rounds of this size have become more common in robotics this year, according to Seed & Series' funding tracker, though the number of robotics seed deals is roughly flat.

articles.author: Marisol Achebe
articles.title: GridLoom secures $80 million Series C co-led by Aster Fund and Halden Growth
articles.summary: Grid-software company GridLoom raised an $80 million Series C co-led by Aster Fund and Halden Growth to expand its software for balancing electricity demand.
articles.content:
GridLoom, which makes software that helps utilities shift electricity demand from homes and businesses to off-peak hours, has raised $80 million in a Series C round co-led by Aster Fund and Halden Growth.

The company says its software manages about 1.2 gigawatts of flexible demand across 14 utilities. Chief executive Hollis Varga said the funding will support expansion to commercial buildings.

GridLoom said it is not yet profitable. The company did not disclose its valuation.

articles.author: Marisol Achebe
articles.title: Copperline Security raises $6.5 million seed round to monitor VPN appliances for intrusions
articles.summary: Cybersecurity startup Copperline Security raised $6.5 million in a seed round from Mosaic Angels Network and Fieldstone Ventures.
articles.content:
Copperline Security, a startup that monitors VPN and remote-access appliances for signs of intrusion, has raised $6.5 million in a seed round from Mosaic Angels Network and Fieldstone Ventures.

The company's founders previously worked on incident response teams. Chief executive Dara Vukovic said recent attacks on remote-access appliances, including the Pallas Gateway flaw flagged by the Civic Cyber Response Center, show how often these devices are the entry point.

Copperline said it has 11 paying customers, most of them school districts and regional hospitals.

articles.author: Nadia Kerrigan
articles.title: Tarnwell Compute raises $220 million Series D led by Orbit Growth Partners to build AI accelerators
articles.summary: AI chip designer Tarnwell Compute raised $220 million in a Series D led by Orbit Growth Partners, with participation from Corvane Ventures, the venture arm of its foundry partner.
articles.content:
Tarnwell Compute, which designs chips for running AI models in data centers, has raised $220 million in a Series D round led by Orbit Growth Partners. Corvane Ventures, the investment arm of Corvane Semiconductor, which manufactures Tarnwell's chips, also participated.

Tarnwell said the money will fund production of its second-generation accelerator on Corvane's 3nm-class process. The company said it has signed customers but declined to disclose revenue.

Corvane's participation links an investor with a supplier relationship, which is common in the chip industry. Tarnwell's production plans depend in part on Corvane reaching its projected capacity at Calder Valley.

articles.author: Tamsin Okafor-Bell
articles.title: AI education startups raised more money in the third quarter, but in fewer deals
articles.summary: Seed & Series' tracker counted $610 million raised by AI education startups across 38 rounds in the third quarter, up 22% by dollars from the second quarter while deal count fell 9%.
articles.content:
Startups building AI tools for education raised $610 million across 38 funding rounds in the third quarter, according to Seed & Series' funding tracker, which logs publicly announced rounds. That was up 22% in dollars from the second quarter, while the number of deals fell 9%.

Larger, later-stage rounds drove the increase, including Quillfield's $45 million Series B. Seed-stage deal counts fell for the second straight quarter.

The tracker includes only announced rounds and may undercount smaller deals. Quarter-to-quarter changes in a small sample can reflect a few large rounds rather than a trend.

articles.author: Elena Brightwater
articles.title: Opinion: Founders, a big round buys time. It is not a verdict on your company
articles.summary: A two-time founder argues that headline round sizes say little about whether a startup has solved a real problem.
articles.content:
Funding announcements are written to sound like victories. The Series B headline tells you that investors were persuaded, not that customers were.

When I read about a round, I look for the things the announcement usually leaves out: how many customers pay, whether they renew, and what the company still needs to prove. Quillfield's chief executive deserves credit for saying plainly that her company has usage data but not yet learning-outcome data.

For aspiring founders, the lesson is to raise what you need to answer your next most important question. This is a personal opinion about building companies; it is not a recommendation to invest in, or avoid, any startup.

articles.author: Markets Integrity Commission Office of Public Affairs
articles.title: Markets Integrity Commission charges Brightvane Advisors with misleading clients about AI use
articles.summary: The Markets Integrity Commission settled charges that Brightvane Advisors falsely marketed portfolios as managed by autonomous AI agents; Brightvane agreed to a $310,000 penalty without admitting or denying the findings.
articles.content:
The Markets Integrity Commission today announced settled charges against Brightvane Advisors LLC, a registered investment adviser, for making false and misleading statements about its use of artificial intelligence, a practice sometimes called “AI washing.”

According to the Commission's order, Brightvane's website and client presentations stated that client portfolios were “managed in real time by autonomous AI agents.” The order finds that Brightvane's portfolios were in fact allocated using a spreadsheet-based model that staff updated quarterly, and that the firm did not use the AI agents it described.

Without admitting or denying the findings, Brightvane agreed to a censure, a civil penalty of $310,000, and to retain an independent compliance consultant to review its marketing materials.

“Advisers who describe AI capabilities to clients must be able to show that those capabilities exist and are used as described,” said Commission enforcement director Harriet Vandermeer.

articles.author: Callum Rourke
articles.title: Regulator fines adviser $310,000 for claiming AI agents it did not use
articles.summary: Brightvane Advisors agreed to pay $310,000 to settle Markets Integrity Commission charges that it marketed autonomous AI portfolio management it did not actually use.
articles.content:
Brightvane Advisors agreed to pay a $310,000 penalty to settle charges by the Markets Integrity Commission that it misled clients by claiming their portfolios were run by autonomous AI agents. According to the regulator, the firm actually used a spreadsheet model updated once a quarter.

Brightvane neither admitted nor denied the findings. The firm said in a statement that it had “updated its marketing to describe its investment process accurately.”

The case is the Commission's first this year focused on exaggerated AI claims. Compliance lawyers said the message to advisers is that marketing language about AI is subject to the same accuracy rules as any other claim.

articles.author: Broker-Dealer Standards Authority
articles.title: Regulatory Notice: BDSA proposes supervision expectations for AI agents at member firms
articles.summary: The Broker-Dealer Standards Authority proposed guidance requiring member firms to inventory AI agents, set authority limits, require human approval for actions beyond those limits, and keep audit trails for three years; comments are due in 60 days.
articles.content:
The Broker-Dealer Standards Authority (BDSA) is requesting comment on proposed guidance for member broker-dealers that use AI agents, meaning software that can plan and take actions such as drafting client communications, flagging suspicious trades, or routing orders.

Who is affected: all member firms that use or plan to use AI agents in customer-facing, surveillance, trading, or operational functions.

What would change: firms would be expected to (1) maintain an inventory of AI agents and their permitted actions; (2) set written authority limits for each agent; (3) require human approval before an agent acts outside those limits; (4) keep audit trails of agent actions for at least three years; and (5) test controls on what data agents can access.

When: comments are due within 60 days. BDSA expects to issue final guidance after reviewing comments, with expectations taking effect six months after the final notice. BDSA noted that existing rules on supervision, communications, and best interest obligations already apply to activity performed with AI tools.

articles.author: Priya Moorcroft
articles.title: Commentary: The AI-washing case is a warning about marketing, not about AI
articles.summary: A former compliance officer argues the Brightvane settlement is about truthful advertising and that firms should audit AI claims as they would any performance claim.
articles.content:
The Brightvane settlement will be read as a story about artificial intelligence. It is really a story about advertising. The firm said it used autonomous AI agents; according to the regulator, it used a spreadsheet.

Firms that do use AI agents should take a different lesson from the BDSA's proposed guidance: be ready to show what your agents do, what they are allowed to do, and who approves exceptions. That documentation is also what makes marketing claims defensible.

This is my opinion as a former compliance officer. It is not legal or investment advice.

articles.author: Civic Cyber Response Center
articles.title: Advisory: Actively exploited authentication bypass in Pallas Gateway VPN appliances
articles.summary: The Civic Cyber Response Center warns that an authentication bypass (tracking ID DEMO-2026-0142) in Pallas Gateway versions 9.2 through 9.4 is being actively exploited; Pallas has released version 9.4.3.
articles.content:
Summary: The Civic Cyber Response Center (CCRC) is aware of active exploitation of an authentication bypass vulnerability, tracked as DEMO-2026-0142, in Pallas Networks' Pallas Gateway VPN appliances, versions 9.2 through 9.4.2. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can obtain an administrative session. Pallas rates the flaw critical (severity score 9.8 of 10).

Affected products: Pallas Gateway 9.2.x, 9.3.x, and 9.4.0 through 9.4.2. Versions 9.1 and earlier are not affected, according to Pallas.

Recommended actions: upgrade to Pallas Gateway 9.4.3 immediately; if upgrading is not possible, disable the web administration interface on internet-facing ports; review logs for administrative logins from unfamiliar addresses since the start of the month; and reset credentials for accounts that authenticate through affected appliances.

CCRC has observed exploitation against education and health-care organizations. This advisory will be updated as more information becomes available.

articles.author: Ada Fenwick
articles.title: Pallas Networks patches VPN flaw already used in attacks on schools and hospitals
articles.summary: Attackers exploited a critical flaw in Pallas Gateway VPN appliances before a patch was available; at least two school districts and one regional hospital network reported intrusions.
articles.content:
Pallas Networks released a security update for its Pallas Gateway VPN appliances after attackers used a critical authentication flaw to break into organizations including at least two school districts and a regional hospital network, according to the Civic Cyber Response Center and the affected organizations.

Pallas said in a statement that it learned of the flaw from a customer and “released a fix within six days.” The company said it has no evidence that customer data was taken from its own systems.

Security researchers at Copperline Security estimated that about 1,900 internet-facing Pallas Gateway devices were still unpatched as of Thursday. That estimate is based on internet scanning and has not been confirmed by Pallas.

The CCRC has urged organizations to upgrade to version 9.4.3 and to reset credentials, because attackers may have captured passwords before the patch.

articles.author: Jules Penhallow
articles.title: Opinion: Patching can't fix how schools buy security appliances
articles.summary: A security columnist argues that repeated VPN appliance breaches reflect procurement and staffing gaps in schools and hospitals, not only vendor bugs.
articles.content:
The Pallas Gateway breaches follow a familiar pattern: an internet-facing appliance, a critical flaw, and organizations without the staff to patch within days. Schools and small hospitals are hit hardest because they buy these devices and then have no one whose job is to watch them.

Vendors should ship fewer critical flaws. But buyers can also demand automatic updates, published patch timelines, and clear end-of-support dates before signing contracts.

This is my opinion. Some security leaders argue that automatic updates create their own risks for critical systems, and that trade-off deserves a real debate.

articles.author: Civic Cyber Response Center
articles.title: Update: Exploitation of Pallas Gateway flaw expands; organizations urged to rotate credentials
articles.summary: CCRC updated its advisory on DEMO-2026-0142: exploitation has expanded to local governments, and attackers are reusing credentials captured before patching.
articles.content:
Update to the Pallas Gateway advisory (tracking ID DEMO-2026-0142): CCRC has observed exploitation expand from education and health-care organizations to local government networks.

In several incidents, attackers used credentials captured from unpatched appliances to log in after the appliances were upgraded. Patching alone does not remove this access. CCRC recommends that all organizations that ran affected versions reset passwords and session tokens for every account that authenticated through the appliance, and review remote-access logs.

CCRC has not attributed the activity to a specific group. The recommended actions in the original advisory remain in effect.

articles.author: Owen Marchetti
articles.title: Quarry Peak warns of tight supply for high-purity process gases as fab expansions accelerate
articles.summary: Specialty gas supplier Quarry Peak said demand for high-purity neon and other process gases could exceed its capacity next year if announced fab expansions proceed on schedule.
articles.content:
Quarry Peak Specialty Gases, a supplier of high-purity gases used in chipmaking, said demand could exceed its production capacity in the second half of next year if fab expansions announced by Corvane Semiconductor and others proceed on schedule.

The company said it is adding purification capacity but that new lines take about 18 months to build. “This is a projection based on our customers' announced plans,” said Quarry Peak's head of supply, Ingrid Solheim. “If expansions slip, so does the crunch.”

Supply-chain analysts described two scenarios: tight supply that raises gas prices and delays some fab ramps, or slower fab expansions that leave current capacity sufficient. Neither is a confirmed outcome.

articles.author: Beatrix Oyelaran
articles.title: Fab expansion drives demand for cleanroom technicians; Calder community colleges add certificates
articles.summary: Three Calder community colleges are launching 16-week cleanroom technician certificates as Corvane's Fab 3 expansion and supplier plants seek about 1,800 new workers.
articles.content:
Three community colleges in Calder will launch 16-week certificate programs for semiconductor cleanroom technicians next semester, citing hiring plans tied to Corvane Semiconductor's Calder Valley expansion.

The programs cover contamination control, equipment maintenance basics, and safety. Corvane has said its expansion will create about 1,800 permanent jobs; the colleges estimate about 40% will be technician roles.

Graduates are not guaranteed jobs, and program leaders said enrollment targets are based on employer projections that could change if expansion timelines shift. Corvane has agreed to interview program graduates but has not committed to a number of hires.

articles.author: Beatrix Oyelaran
articles.title: Survey: 61% of manufacturers plan to retrain inspectors for AI-assisted quality control
articles.summary: An Industrial Skills Council survey of 412 manufacturers found 61% plan to retrain quality inspectors to work with AI vision systems within two years; the figures reflect stated plans, not completed programs.
articles.content:
Sixty-one percent of manufacturers surveyed by the Industrial Skills Council said they plan to retrain quality inspectors to work alongside AI-assisted vision systems within two years. The council surveyed 412 manufacturing companies; responses reflect companies' stated plans, not completed training.

Respondents most often cited skills in interpreting AI flags, adjusting inspection thresholds, and basic data analysis. Only 18% said they expect to reduce the number of inspectors; most said roles would change rather than disappear.

The council said smaller manufacturers were less likely to have a retraining budget. The survey was conducted online and respondents were self-selected, so results may not represent all manufacturers.

articles.author: Wendell Marsh-Adeyemi
articles.title: Column: Apprenticeships, not short courses, will staff the fab boom
articles.summary: A columnist argues that paid apprenticeships with employers will do more than short certificates to fill technician roles at new fabs.
articles.content:
Calder's new cleanroom certificates are a good start. But semiconductor technicians learn most of their job on the line, under supervision, with equipment no college can afford to buy.

Paid apprenticeships, in which employers share the cost of training and commit to hiring, give workers a clearer path and give companies people who already know their tools. Corvane and its suppliers are well placed to offer them.

This is my view. College leaders argue, fairly, that certificates reach people faster and that apprenticeships depend on employers' willingness to commit.
